name: Finding the Number of Days Above the Average Temperature
description: Construct a program that reads a series of temperatures and reports the average temperature and the number of the days that are above the average. Assume that the input values could have a decimal point.
code:
#Step 1: Read the number of days that we have to enter their temperature data
num_days = int(input("Enter the number of temperature values that will be entered: "))
#Step 2: Read the temperature values
temps = []
total = 0
for i in range(num_days):
    val = float(input("Enter the temperature: "))
    temps.append(val)
    total += val
#Step 3: Calculate the average temperature
average = 0
if num_days == 0:
    print("No temperature values were entered.")
else:
    average = total / num_days
#Step 4: Count the number of the days that are above the average temperature
above = 0
for x in temps:
    if x > average:
        above += 1
#Step 5: Display the results
print("Average temperature:", average)
print(above, "days above average.")

commentList:
We need to first ask the user how many days of temperature data will be provided. To read the user input from command line, we use the input() function. This statement prints a text on the screen "Enter the number of temperature values that will be entered: ", then reads the text entered by the user.

The value that will be read is a string and we need to convert it to a int. We convert the input string to its integer representation by using the int() function.
Note that we do not necessarily have to store the returned value from the input function in a variable. We could use the input function call directly as the int function parameter.

Note that the conversion to integer can only be done if the string actually presents a number. If the input number is a float, the int() function cuts off the fractional part of the floating-point number to create an integer.

We first need to define a list referred by variable temps for storing the temperatures that the user provides. We initialize it with an empty list and will later use the function append to add each temperature value to it. We need this list later to iterate over the temperature values and calculate the number of the days that are above the average.
We need variable total to maintain a running total, which means the sum of the temperature values that the user has entered so far. Of course, the total should be initialized with 0.

We want to read each temperature value and calculate the running total for the temperature values that the user has entered so far.

We also need to add each temperature value in the list to later count the number of days that are above the average. Therefore, we use a for loop to iterate over the list indexes and add a temperature value to each index.

We need the list indexes to have a length of num_days and start at 0 with every integer number up to but not including num_days, where variable num_days is the number of days for which the user will provide the temperature values. We get this sequence by calling the range(num_days) function.
Note that all statements inside the loop need to be indented with respect to the loop header.

We need to read the temperature value that the user enters. To read the user input from command line, we use the input() function. This statement prints a text on the screen "Enter the temperature: ", then reads the text entered by the user.

The value that will be read is a string and we need to convert it to a float. We convert the input string to its float representation by using the float() function.

The conversion of the value from string to float can only be done if the string could be translated into a valid floating-point value. Also note that we do not necessarily have to store the returned value from the input function in a variable. We could use the input function call directly as the float function parameter.
We want to add the temperature value that the user has entered to the list. To do this, in each iteration, we call the function append() to add the value read to the end of the list.

We need to add each value read to the running total that is stored in variable total. So, in each iteration, we add the value read stored in variable val to the variable total and store the result into the variable total.

The += operator adds the value of variable val to the value of the variable total and the result is stored in the variable total. Thus, this statement is equivalent to the statement total = total + val.
We need variable average to store the average of the temperature values that the user has entered.
We need the if statement before computing the average to avoid a divide-by-zero error. This occurs if the user enters 0 for the number of days.
If the user enters 0 for the number of days, then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.
This statement prints the text "No temperature values were entered." to the default standard output stream. This text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.

If the first test fails (i.e., when the user enters a positive number greater than zero for the number of days), then the body of the previous if statement will not be executed, instead the body of this else statement will be executed.
We need to calculate the average by dividing the sum of the temperature values by the number of the days that we received their temperature values.
Notice that the / operator performs the real division, producing a floating point result.

We want to iterate over the list and count the number of temperature values that are above the average. We traverse the list values using for loop because for loop can step across any kind of sequence object including lists.
This for loop assigns the name x to each of the values in the list in turn, from left to right, and then the statements in the loop body will be executed for each.
Note that all statements inside the loop need to be indented with respect to the loop header.

We need to compare the list value that we visited with the average of temperature values stored in variable average. If that value is greater than the average, then we need to increase the number of days above average by 1.
If visited value in the list is greater than the average, then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.
When the current temperature value is greater than the average, then we have to increment the number of days above the average by 1.
The += operator adds 1 to the value of variable above and the result is stored into the variable above. Therefore, it is functionally equivalent to the statement above = above + 1.
